content: Sam planted beans in a pot by the window. He watered them every morning. After ten days, two small green leaves came up. Sam showed them to his grandmother.
Every day, Aditi takes the red bus to school. The bus stops at the post office. Her friend Joy gets on there. They sit together at the back.

On Saturday, Grandpa took Leela to the market. They bought onions, tomatoes and a big watermelon.

On the way home, it started to rain. Grandpa opened his black umbrella, and they shared it. The watermelon was so heavy that Leela had to rest twice.

The science club meets on Tuesdays after lunch. Last week the club planned to visit the museum on Friday. But the bus was not free, so the trip moved to the following Monday. Mrs Rao asked everyone to bring a notebook and a packed lunch.
Priya found a little grey kitten under the stairs. It was cold and hungry. She gave it some warm milk in a blue bowl. Now the kitten sleeps on her bed.
Our school played a football match against Green Hill School. It was a hot day. Our team scored three goals and Green Hill scored one. Farhan scored the last goal with his head.

In the morning, Class 4 visited the zoo. First they saw the elephants having a bath. Then they watched the monkeys swing from branch to branch.

At noon, they ate lunch under a big neem tree. After lunch, a keeper showed them how he feeds the tortoises. He gave them lettuce and pieces of pumpkin.

Arun thought he had left his pencil box in the classroom. He looked under his desk and inside his bag, but it was not there. Then his sister remembered seeing it on the kitchen table that morning. It was there, next to the bread.
Dark clouds filled the sky. Maya ran to bring the clothes in from the line. She was just in time. A minute later, the rain came down hard.

For his birthday, Raj got a green bicycle with a silver bell. At first he kept falling off.

His older sister held the back of the seat while he pedalled. After a week, she let go without telling him. Raj rode all the way to the end of the lane on his own.
Mina borrowed a book about volcanoes on Monday. She had to return it in two weeks. She finished it in four days and returned it early, on Friday, so that her friend could read it.
There is a mango tree outside our house. In summer it gives us sweet mangoes. Birds build nests in its branches. On hot days, we sit in its shade.

Ben wanted to make a cake for his mother. He mixed flour, sugar and eggs. But he forgot to turn on the oven! When he noticed, he laughed, turned it on, and waited. The cake was late, but his mother loved it.

Camels can live in the desert for many days without water. They store fat in their humps, which their bodies can use for energy.

Camels also have long eyelashes and can close their noses. This keeps out the sand when the wind blows.

Many children in our town walk to school. Walking is good exercise, and it is cheaper than taking a bus.

But the roads near the school are busy in the morning. The town council has decided to paint new crossings and to put a guard at the main gate.
Brush your teeth twice a day, in the morning and at night. Use a small amount of toothpaste. Brush for two minutes. Clean teeth stay strong and healthy.
Lalita found a baby bird on the ground. It could not fly yet. She called her father, who gently put it back in its nest. The next day, the mother bird was feeding it.

Honey is made by bees from the nectar of flowers. They carry the nectar back to the hive and store it in wax cells.

People have eaten honey for thousands of years. It was used to sweeten food long before sugar was common, and some people still use it as a medicine for sore throats.

Our class wanted to help the birds near our school. We put out bowls of water on the roof during the hot months.

At first, only crows came. After a week, sparrows, mynas and even a kingfisher came to drink. Now we keep a list of every bird we see.
In January, the sky over our city fills with kites. People fly them from rooftops. Some kites are shaped like birds. Everyone shouts when a kite is cut.
Nikhil practised the drum every evening for a month. At first his family covered their ears. On the day of the school concert, he played without a single mistake, and everyone clapped.

Snakes cannot hear sounds the way we do. They have no outer ears.

Instead, snakes feel movements in the ground. When a person walks nearby, a snake can feel the steps through its body.

content:
Meena's new kite was red and yellow, with a long blue tail. On Saturday morning she took it to the field behind her school. The wind was strong, and the kite rose higher than the coconut trees. Suddenly the string snapped. Meena watched the kite drift over the wall and disappear.

She walked home slowly, kicking a stone along the road. Her little brother Arjun was waiting at the gate. When he saw her empty hands, he did not say anything. He went inside and came back with his own small paper kite. "You can fly mine," he said. Meena smiled for the first time that morning.

content:
On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. Scientists call this the urban heat island effect.

There are several reasons for it. Roads, roofs and car parks are made of dark materials such as asphalt and concrete, which absorb sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly at night. Cities also have fewer trees and fields. Plants cool the air around them by releasing water through their leaves, so when green spaces are replaced by buildings, this natural cooling is lost. Finally, cars, air conditioners and factories all produce heat of their own.

Some cities are trying to fight back. Singapore has added gardens to the roofs and walls of tall buildings, and in some Indian cities people are painting their roofs white so that they reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it. These changes are small, but together they can make a real difference to how hot a city feels.

content:
Kavya had rehearsed her answers so often that she could recite them in her sleep. Yet when the door of the principal's office opened and her name was called, every carefully polished sentence seemed to dissolve.

The panel consisted of three teachers, one of whom, Mr. Iyer, had once returned her science project with the single word "Ambitious" written across the top. She had never decided whether it was a compliment.

"Why do you want to lead the school magazine?" he asked, without looking up from his papers.

Kavya opened her mouth to deliver her prepared answer about teamwork and deadlines. Instead she heard herself say, "Because every month I read it and wish it were braver."

There was a pause. Mr. Iyer put down his pen and, for the first time, looked directly at her. "Go on," he said.

Tara has a small brown dog. His name is Bobby. Every morning, Tara and Bobby walk to the shop.

One day, Bobby ran after a cat. Tara could not see him. She sat down and cried. Then she heard a bark. Bobby was behind the shop, next to the milk van.

Tara hugged him. "Never run away again," she said. Bobby wagged his tail.

content:
Kiran had worked on her volcano for two weeks. She had made it from newspaper and glue, painted it brown and green, and practised the eruption three times at home. Each time, red foam had bubbled out of the top perfectly.

On the morning of the science fair, Kiran's little brother Dev knocked the volcano off the table. One side cracked open. Dev's eyes filled with tears. "I'm sorry," he whispered.

Kiran wanted to shout, but she looked at Dev's face and took a deep breath. "We can fix it," she said. They found some tape and an old box, and Dev held the pieces while Kiran stuck them together.

At the fair, the volcano did not look as neat as before, but when Kiran added the vinegar, the foam rushed out. The judges laughed and clapped. Later, Kiran told them that her brother had helped her. Dev stood up very straight and smiled for the rest of the day.

skill: Locates explicit detail, Identifies the main idea
content:
In late spring, a crowded honeybee colony may split in two. The old queen leaves with about half of the workers, and the swarm hangs from a branch while it searches for a new home. The search can last from a few hours to several days.

The queen does not choose the new home. Instead, a few hundred older bees, called scouts, fly out to inspect possible sites such as hollow trees. A good site must be dry, well above the ground and large enough to store honey for the winter. When a scout returns, she performs a "waggle dance" on the surface of the swarm. The angle of the dance shows the direction of the site, and its length shows the distance.

Scouts that have found better sites dance for longer and with more energy, so more bees go to inspect those sites. Over time, support gathers around one location. When enough scouts are waiting at the same site, the whole swarm takes off and flies there. Researchers have found that swarms usually choose the best site available, even though no single bee compares all the options. Some scientists believe human committees could learn from the way bees reach agreement.

passage: The Map in My Grandfather's Drawer
content:
My grandfather kept a map in the top drawer of his desk, folded so many times that the creases had worn into white lines. It showed the district where he grew up, and he had marked it in pencil: a school, a well, a banyan tree, and a house that he labelled only with an initial. When I asked about the house, he said it belonged to "people we knew", and changed the subject with the practised ease of a man who had done it many times before.

After he died, my mother and I drove to the district with the map. Most of what he had marked was gone. The school had become a bank; the well had been filled in and paved over. Only the banyan tree remained, its aerial roots now so thick that it looked less like a tree than a small, untidy forest. We found the house, too, or what was left of it: two walls and a doorway opening onto nothing.

A woman from the next street told us that the family who had lived there had moved away decades ago. She remembered a boy who used to wait by the doorway every evening. She did not know his name.

I used to think a map was a record of places. Now I suspect it is closer to a record of attention: it shows what someone could not stop looking at. My grandfather's map was not out of date. It was accurate about the only thing it had ever tried to describe.

Adding -s, -ed and -ing
Most words just take the ending. The base word does not change: look → looks, looked, looking.
Example: kick → kicks, kicked, kicking
Example: help → helps, helped, helping
Tip: Say the base word first, then add the ending you hear.
Check: Which is correct? (paint + -ing) Options: paintting / painting / painteing
key: painting: paint + -ing = painting. Nothing changes in paint.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
Adding -es
Words ending in s, x, z, ch or sh add -es, because you can hear an extra syllable: fox → foxes, catch → catches.
Example: dress → dresses
Example: brush → brushes (you can hear 'brush-iz')
Tip: If you can hear an extra 'iz' sound at the end, write -es.
Check: Which is correct? (church + -s/-es) Options: churchs / churches / churchies
key: churches: church ends in ch, so it takes -es: churches.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
Doubling the last letter (short words)
In a one-syllable word with one short vowel and one final consonant, double the consonant before -ing, -ed, -er or -est: plan → planning, drop → dropped, thin → thinner.
Example: grab → grabbing
Example: hop → hopped (not hoped, which comes from hope)
Tip: Two consonants keep the vowel short: hopping (short o), hoping (long o).
Check: Which is correct? (sit + -ing) Options: siting / sitting / sitteing
key: sitting: sit has one short vowel and one final consonant, so the t doubles: sitting.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
Dropping the silent e
If a word ends in a silent e, drop the e before an ending that starts with a vowel (-ing, -ed, -er): bake → baking, smile → smiling.
Example: ride → riding
Example: dance → dancing
Tip: Keep the e before an ending that starts with a consonant: hope → hopeful.
Check: Which is correct? (write + -ing) Options: writeing / writting / writing
key: writing: write ends in a silent e, which is dropped before -ing: writing.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
Changing y to i
If a word ends in a consonant + y, change the y to i before -ed, -er, -est or -es: hurry → hurried, funny → funniest, lady → ladies.
Example: fry → fried
Example: busy → busier
Tip: Keep the y before -ing (crying), and after a vowel (play → played).
Check: Which is correct? (try + -ed) Options: tryed / tried / tride
key: tried: try ends in consonant + y, so the y changes to i: tried.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
Doubling in longer words
In a longer word, double the last consonant only if the last syllable is stressed: permit → permitted, refer → referred.
Example: admit → admitted (ad-MIT: stress at the end)
Example: regret → regretting
Tip: Say the word aloud and listen for which syllable is strongest.
Check: Which is correct? (commit + -ed) Options: comited / committed / commited
key: committed: com-MIT is stressed on the last syllable, so the t doubles: committed.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
When not to double
If the stress is on the first syllable, do not double: limit → limited, enter → entering, offer → offered.
Example: happen → happened (HAP-pen: stress at the start)
Example: cover → covering
Tip: Compare: preFER → preferred, but OFfer → offered.
Check: Which is correct? (garden + -ing) Options: gardenning / gardening / gardining
key: gardening: GAR-den is stressed on the first syllable, so the n does not double: gardening.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
Tricky endings
Three patterns to learn: ie becomes y before -ing (die → dying); add k after a final c (mimic → mimicked); and in British spelling, a final l after one vowel doubles (travel → travelled).
Example: die → dying
Example: mimic → mimicking
Example: cancel → cancelled (American spelling: canceled)
Tip: OpenPath teaches British spelling, and also accepts American spellings as correct.
Check: Which is correct? (tie + -ing) Options: tieing / tying / tiing
key: tying: tie ends in ie, which becomes y before -ing: tying.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
He, she, it + -s
In the present simple, add -s or -es to the verb after he, she, it or one person or thing: she sings, he fixes, the dog barks.
Example: My aunt teaches music.
Example: It rains a lot in July.
Tip: I, you, we, they: no -s (they play).
Check: Choose: She ___ to music every evening. Options: listen / listens
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
Plural subjects
A plural subject takes a plural verb: the mice run, the trees grow, my cousins live nearby.
Example: The birds are on the roof.
Example: These shoes look new.
Tip: Find the subject first, then match the verb to it.
Check: Choose: The people ___ waiting. Options: is / are
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
Two subjects with and
Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb: Anil and Sara are friends.
Example: My sister and I walk to school.
Example: Bread and butter is… (but a single dish can be singular)
Tip: and adds the subjects together, so the verb is plural.
Check: Choose: Tom and his dog ___ in the park. Options: is / are
key: are: Tom and his dog = two: are.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
Words between subject and verb
The verb agrees with the subject, not with a noun just before it: The jar of sweets is empty. The cup of tea is hot.
Example: The colour of the flowers is bright.
Example: The boys in the team are tired.
Tip: Cover the words between: 'The box … is'.
Check: Choose: The basket of eggs ___ full. Options: is / are
key: is: The subject is the basket (one): is.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
Each, every, everyone
each, every, everyone, nobody and somebody take a singular verb: Each of the girls has a ticket. Everyone is here.
Example: Every child needs sleep.
Example: Somebody is at the door.
Tip: Each of the… is still one at a time: singular.
Check: Choose: Each of the players ___ a shirt. Options: have / has
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
either … or, neither … nor
With either … or and neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the driver nor the passengers were hurt. Either the girls or their father is coming.
Example: Either my parents or my aunt is coming.
Example: Neither the dog nor the cats were hungry.
Tip: Look at the subject closest to the verb.
Check: Choose: Neither Priya nor her brothers ___ at home. Options: is / are
key: are: The nearer subject, brothers, is plural: are.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
Inverted order; a number of
When the verb comes first, find the subject after it: There are many birds. Here comes the bus. 'A number of' is plural; 'the number of' is singular.
Example: A number of shops were closed.
Example: The number of cars is growing.
Tip: Turn the sentence round: many birds are there.
Check: Choose: There ___ three books on the desk. Options: is / are
key: are: The subject is three books: are.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
a or an
Use an before a word that starts with a vowel (a, e, i, o, u) and a before a consonant: an orange, an egg, a ball, a cat.
Example: an inkpot, an onion
Example: a pencil, a dog
Tip: Say it aloud: 'an apple' is easier to say than 'a apple'.
Check: Choose: She ate ___ egg. Options: a / an
key: an: egg starts with a vowel: an egg.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
a first, then the
Use a when you first mention something, then the when you mention it again: I found a shell. The shell was pink. Use a before a job: He is a farmer.
Example: We bought a kite. The kite was red.
Example: My uncle is a doctor.
Tip: a = one of many; the = the one we both know about.
Check: Choose: My father is ___ engineer. Options: the / an / —
key: an: Use a or an before a job: an engineer.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
a or an by sound
Choose a or an by the first sound, not the first letter: an honour (silent h), an MP; a unicorn, a one-rupee coin (they start with 'yoo' and 'w' sounds).
Example: an honour
Example: a uniform, a European city
Tip: Listen to the sound at the start, not the letter.
Check: Choose: She wore ___ uniform. Options: a / an
key: a: uniform starts with a 'yoo' sound: a uniform.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
the for one of a kind
Use the for things there is only one of, or that everyone knows: the moon, the sky, the Prime Minister.
Example: The sky is clear today.
Example: Close the door, please. (the door we both know)
Tip: If there is only one, it is the.
Check: Choose: ___ moon is bright tonight. Options: A / The
key: The: There is only one moon: the moon.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
No a with uncountable nouns
Some nouns cannot be counted: luggage, bread, water, news, rice. Do not use a or an with them: some luggage, a piece of bread.
Example: We bought some bread.
Example: There is a lot of traffic today.
Tip: If you cannot put a number in front of it, do not use a or an.
Check: Choose: I need ___ help. Options: an / some
key: some: help is uncountable here: some help.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
General statements
For general statements about all of something, use no article with plurals and abstract nouns: Elephants are strong. Kindness is important.
Example: Dogs are loyal.
Example: Patience is useful.
Tip: Talking about all of them, in general? No article.
Check: Choose: ___ kindness matters. Options: The / — / A
key: —: A general, abstract idea: no article.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
Articles with names
Most names of people, cities and countries have no article (Delhi, India), but rivers, oceans and some countries do: the Yamuna, the Indian Ocean, the United States. Mountains do not: Mount Abu.
Example: We sailed on the Yamuna.
Example: We visited Mount Abu.
Tip: Rivers, seas and oceans take the.
Check: Choose: ___ Pacific is the largest ocean. Options: — / The / A
key: The: Oceans take the: the Pacific.
status: existing lesson, examples revised in PR #24

content:
Finding a fact
To answer a who, what, where or when question, find the sentence that answers it. The answer is written in the text.
Example: Text: "Ravi keeps his cricket bat under his bed." Question: Where is the bat? Answer: under his bed. (worked example: the sentence tells us)
Example: Where needs a place. Who needs a person. When needs a time.
Tip: Read the question first, then look back in the text for the answer.
Check: Text: "Nisha's cat is called Snowy. Snowy is black." What colour is Snowy? Options: white / black / grey
key: black: The text says 'Snowy is black'. The name sounds white, but the text tells us the colour.

content:
Finding details in a longer text
In a longer text, use the question to find the right paragraph first, then the right sentence.
Example: Question: What did they eat for lunch? Look for the paragraph about lunch, then the sentence with the food. (worked example)
Tip: Look for a word from the question, then read the whole sentence around it.
Check: Text: "In the morning we swam in the river. In the afternoon we ate rice and dal under a tree." What did they eat? Options: fish / rice and dal / fruit
key: rice and dal: The afternoon sentence tells us: rice and dal.

content:
Words that look right
Some answers repeat words from the text but do not answer the question. Check that your answer really answers it.
Example: Text: "The party was planned for Sunday, but it rained, so it was held on Monday." When was the party held? Answer: Monday. Sunday was only the plan. (worked example)
Tip: Ask: does this answer the question, or does it just use the same words?
Check: Text: "We wanted to go to the beach, but the car broke down, so we went to the park." Where did they go? Options: the beach / the park / the garage
key: the park: They wanted the beach, but they went to the park.

content:
What is it mostly about?
The topic is what the whole text is about. Choose the answer that fits every sentence, not just one.
Example: A text gives a dog's name, what it eats and where it sleeps. It is mostly about the dog, not about its food. (worked example)
Tip: A detail is true, but too small. The topic covers everything.
Check: Text: "Our school has a big library. It has books about animals, space and stories. We can borrow two books a week." What is it mostly about? Options: books about space / our school library / borrowing two books
key: our school library: Every sentence is about the library; the others are details.

content:
Choosing the best title
A good title fits the whole story. A title made from one detail is usually too small.
Example: Story: a boy loses his shoe, looks everywhere, and his dog brings it back. Best title: The Dog Who Found the Shoe, not A Red Shoe. (worked example)
Tip: Say the story in one sentence. The best title matches that sentence.
Check: Text: "Ana's balloon flew away. She cried. Her friend shared his balloon, and they played together." Best title? Options: A Red Balloon / A Kind Friend / Playing Outside
key: A Kind Friend: The story is about the friend's kindness.

content:
The main idea of a paragraph
Each paragraph has one big idea. The other sentences give details about it. Find the idea the other sentences support.
